outcome: No accepted resolution of the existence question and no accepted bound move on it has appeared since 26 January 2024; the window holds partial results (bounds conditional on existence, restricted-form theorems, a five-branch case closure, an undated computational lower-bound extension) and several unrefereed claims of full nonexistence, none engaged with by a named specialist, and the problem is still described as open by Wikipedia and by MathWorld (updated 2 October 2026).
problem_asks: One question: does there exist an odd positive integer N with σ(N) = 2N, i.e. N equal to the sum of its proper divisors (an odd perfect number)? Parts: (1) existence, answered by exhibiting one; or (2) nonexistence, answered by proving none exists. The statement asks for nothing else. Size bounds, prime-factor counts, Euler-form restrictions and results on the smallest prime factor are constraints on any such N; they do not answer (1) or (2). The statement is Wikipedia's January 2024 wording, which is this standard question.

events.directly_checkable: The Lean files are the check. As read: file 1 (opn_final_collapse) takes p ≥ 5, 2·p·m² = (p+1)(m²+m+1) and 2m ≥ p+1 (labelled 'The Mandate') and concludes False. File 2 (opn_final_collapse_general) takes p ≥ 5, p = 2k+1, m² ≥ k+1, s_m2 > m²+m, 2(p^k·m²) = s_pk·s_m2 and s_pk > 2p^k and concludes False, with s_pk and s_m2 otherwise unconstrained natural numbers.
events.doubts: (1) Formal statement versus the problem: neither file mentions σ, divisor sums, the equation σ(N) = 2N, or N itself. The hypotheses are reduced relations in ℕ, including one labelled as an assumption (2m ≥ p+1, or m² ≥ k+1). So the verified statement, as read, is not the odd-perfect-number condition. Whether the paper derives these hypotheses from σ(N) = 2N is what the paper's text would have to show; I did not read the paper body. (2) The record is an unreviewed preprint; no named reviewer or commenter found. (3) The repository lists llms.txt among its files; the record says nothing about whether an AI assisted with the Lean code, so I have not treated it as AI involvement.

events.what_happened: Francis Henry Ortiz Hidalgo (Universidad Nacional Santiago Antúnez de Mayolo; ORCID on the record), 'Demostración de la Inexistencia de Números Impares Perfectos', Zenodo record 19058072 (published 17 Mar 2026; last modified 31 Mar 2026; v1; Spanish). The abstract states: 'Se presenta una demostración de que no existen números impares perfectos.' The stated method is the canonical prime factorisation of a hypothetical N, the structure of σ(N) = 2N, and the impossibility of N ≡ 1 (mod 6) under the constraints derived. The PDF was not in the fetched content. Opened the Zenodo record only.

events.doubts: The argument was not read: the PDF was not in the fetched content. Self-published. The abstract names N ≡ 1 (mod 6) as the contradiction without showing how the constraints yield it, on the record I read.

events.what_happened: Marco Mantovanelli, 'Certified Minimal-Prime Branch Closures for Odd Perfect Numbers', arXiv 2607.04365 (submitted 5 Jul 2026; one version). Theorem 1.1, quoted from the arXiv HTML: 'there is no odd perfect number with min{p:p∣N}∈{5,7,11,13,17}'. The paper says: 'It is not an unconditional proof that odd perfect numbers do not exist', and 'The cases q=3 and q≥19 remain outside the scope of this paper.' Method: the exact q-adic valuation balance for σ(N) = 2N, with the claim that smaller primes cannot divide N, and finite computations packaged as certificate files, Python verifier scripts and SHA256 hashes (frozen release C-small-2026-07). The q = 5 branch is the detailed model; q = 7, 11, 13, 17 follow the same mechanism. I opened the arXiv abstract page and the HTML, which truncates after Section 11 (Closure of the q=11 Branch), so the Conclusion and Acknowledgements were not read. The arXiv PDF returned binary.
events.revisions: v1 only (5 Jul 2026).
events.delivers: No odd perfect number whose smallest prime factor is 5, 7, 11, 13 or 17, i.e. five of the minimal-prime branches, relative to the author's verifier contract. The paper excludes the q = 3 branch and all q ≥ 19 branches, and says it does not prove nonexistence.
events.remains: The q = 3 branch, the q ≥ 19 branches, and therefore the general question.

checked_by.what_they_did: Review dated 11 Jul 2026. Verdict: 'Solid, scoped computer-assisted closures of five least-prime OPN branches'. Three major objections: inventory completeness (the master wrappers check only the listed records); opaque tail parameters B = 59 and M = 18; and q = 5 pure and post-window closures that rely on Zsigmondy primitive divisors and endpoint inequalities. Five minor objections.

events.time_since_posted: about three months; no human engagement found

machine_checked.note: Certificate files and verifier scripts are described as ancillary files; I did not download or run them.

events.doubts: The paper's own statement is that it does not prove nonexistence. The automated referee's major objections are listed above and are unanswered in the record I can see. The inventory-completeness concern rests on the wrappers checking only listed records.
events.direction: Cuts toward nonexistence for five minimal-prime branches only. Partial: the question as posed is not answered.

events.what_happened: Pascal Ochem and Joshua Zelinsky, 'On odd perfect numbers with exactly one even exponent greater than 2', arXiv 2607.19746 (submitted 22 Jul 2026; one version). The abstract states: 'We show that if all the even exponents of an odd perfect number N are equal to 2 except for one, then 3^(23,000,000,000) divides N.' The claim is conditional on that exponent pattern and does not assert or deny existence. I opened the arXiv abstract page and the Pith review; the full text was not read.
events.revisions: v1 only.
events.delivers: Within the class of odd perfect numbers whose even exponents are all 2 except one: 3^(23,000,000,000) divides N. Nothing outside that class, and nothing on existence.
events.remains: Existence and nonexistence in general, and every odd perfect number outside the stated exponent pattern.

checked_by.what_they_did: Review dated 1 Aug 2026. Verdict opens 'Genuine jump from q ≥ 16 to q ≥ 23,000,000,000 for restrained OPNs, mostly solid' and continues 'but the final numerical product uses a factor that does not match the quoted program output'; ends 'needs correction before the bound is trusted'. Three major issues: an abundancy factor mismatch in §4 (1.088507187872 in the text vs 1.076855990994 in the product); reliance on a three-week sieve described only in pseudocode, with no logs or checksums; and Lemma 8 cited from external results without theorem numbers. Four minor issues.

events.time_since_posted: about three months; no human engagement found
events.doubts: The automated referee's major objections, listed above, are specific: a numerical factor in the final product does not match the program output quoted in the text, the sieve result is unverified, and Lemma 8 is not self-contained. I have not checked these myself, and the paper body was not read. The review states that no human has reviewed the paper.
events.direction: Restricted-class divisibility result. No direction on existence.

disputes.summary: The 10^2200 and Ω(N) ≥ 115 extension is attributed by MathWorld to 'Ochem (2026)'. The only source I could open for it is Ochem's undated project page, whose composite-file markers are dated 2/2025. No paper or talk was found, so the date and the authorship of the computation are both unresolved.

Two search snippets assign the same preprint title, 'A Note on Odd Perfect Numbers', to Frank Vega on Preprints.org, and disagree on its scope (a full nonexistence claim versus nonexistence for odd perfect numbers not divisible by 3) and on its date (October 2024 from the ID, July 2025 from another snippet). The Preprints.org page was not reachable, so the record cannot be resolved.

A scraped aggregator page lists a 'Do odd perfect numbers exist?' item beside an OpenAI announcement, and an unverified snippet repeats it. Nothing in OpenAI's own repository index (openai/math CONTENTS.md, read in full) lists an odd-perfect-number manuscript, so the link is unsupported.

summary: Since 26 January 2024 the problem has not been settled by any accepted argument, and I found no accepted move on the existence question itself. The Wikipedia article (opened) still says it is unknown whether any odd perfect numbers exist and still gives the 10^1500 and 10-prime bounds; MathWorld (opened, updated 2 October 2026) gives the same existence status and attributes an extension to 10^2200 and 115 prime factors to 'Ochem (2026)'. The in-window events fall into three groups. (a) Partial results that make no existence claim: Zelinsky (arXiv 2402.14234, Feb 2024; bounds that assume existence), Stone (Integers 2024; dates and results from a journal-front-matter snippet, PDF unopened), Yamada's restricted-form theorem (arXiv 2312.17059, posted Dec 2023, revised Feb 2024, published IJPAM 2025; a pre-window date, so not in-window as an event), Bërdëllima (Elemente 2025; abstract not read), Shiraishi's modulo-3 constraint (Dec 2025), Rodgers (conditional on abc and an unproved lemma), Tóth (an analogue: odd spoof multiperfect numbers, not odd perfect numbers), Ochem and Zelinsky (arXiv 22 July 2026; restricted to exponent patterns with all even exponents 2 except one, giving 3^(23,000,000,000) | N; an automated referee flags a numerical factor mismatch and an unverified sieve), and Mantovanelli (arXiv 5 July 2026; closes the smallest-prime branches q = 5, 7, 11, 13, 17; the author states it is not an unconditional nonexistence proof and excludes q = 3 and q ≥ 19; an automated referee calls it 'solid, scoped' with three major objections). (b) A computational extension on Ochem's undated project page: N > 10^2200 and Ω(N) ≥ 115, with composite files marked 2/2025 and no paper found. (c) Unrefereed full-nonexistence claims: Shiraishi (Zenodo 18409975, 29 Jan 2026, 'purely structural'; the same author's 18217948 of 12 Jan 2026 proves only the 13⁵ m² case, so the claimed scope grew in 17 days); Reed (Zenodo 18351748, 23 Jan 2026, for p ≥ 5, which by Euler's form covers every Euler prime, with a Lean 4 repository; I read no sorry, admit, axiom or native_decide in the two files but did not compile them, and as read their theorems take reduced arithmetic relations as hypotheses (for example 2·p·m² = (p+1)(m²+m+1) and 2m ≥ p+1 labelled 'The Mandate'), with nothing mentioning σ(N) = 2N, divisor sums or N, so the formal check does not yet reach the problem's condition); Liu (preprints.ru, 14 Jan 2026, not peer-reviewed; the abstract gives no step from its premise); Ortiz Hidalgo (Zenodo, 17 Mar 2026, Spanish; PDF not read); Vega (Preprints.org 202410.0547, 2024 or 2025, unresolved; the page was blocked); and pre-window claims by Davis (2004, v3 2008), Saeid-Nia (arXiv 2101.07176, 2021; v4 2023), Violi (SSRN 2023), a Cambridge Open Engage preprint (December 2023) and Vega's 2022 EasyChair conditional note, plus Figshare (April 2025, conditional on two conjectures; blocked). None of the unrefereed claims has a named specialist engaging with it that I could find; the only public engagement comes from automated referees. On AI: OpenAI's 722-manuscript release (openai/math; CONTENTS.md read in full across seven windows, 719 manuscripts after three withdrawals) has no entry on perfect numbers; the 'Do odd perfect numbers exist?' item on an aggregator page is unsupported. DeepMind's AlphaEvolve impact post (7 May 2026) and Epoch's FrontierMath open-problems overview both omit the problem, and searches on GPT-5, Claude and the AI trackers found no odd-perfect result. The one AI-named item is the acknowledgements of Mantovanelli's arXiv 2607.04365, which I could not open. A search snippet (not verified) reports that the acknowledgements say ChatGPT 5.5 (OpenAI) helped with LaTeX formatting, language refinement, literature search, proof presentation and coding support, and that the author takes responsibility for the mathematics. If that wording is confirmed, those are writing and search aids rather than load-bearing mathematics, so ai.systems is empty and none_found is false; the 'coding support' item is the one to check against the verifier scripts, since the closures rest on them. The Pith reviews are AI referees, not authors, and are recorded as automated checks. Close calls: (i) the 10^2200 extension moves a bound on N, but it has no paper and bounds no quantity the problem names, so it is a finite-range check; (ii) Mantovanelli's closures are a case split on the problem's own smallest-prime parameter, so they move the problem's own quantity, but they leave q = 3 and q ≥ 19 open; (iii) Stone's and Zelinsky's bounds are conditional on existence, so they constrain any odd perfect number without moving the existence question.
competing_reading: Read the Reed files as a sorry-free formal verification of nonexistence for every Euler prime, on the view that the reduced hypotheses are the paper's own derivation from σ(N) = 2N, which the record cannot confirm. Read Mantovanelli's five-branch closure and the Ochem–Zelinsky exponent-class bound as moves in the problem's own quantities (smallest prime factor and exponent structure), which would make this window a real, if partial, advance. Read the 10^2200 extension as a moved size bound on any odd perfect number, since it is the threshold the problem's own objects must clear. Against each: none is peer-reviewed; the Lean statements as read do not contain the problem's condition; the Mantovanelli and Ochem–Zelinsky papers draw specific objections from automated referees and the authors state that they do not prove nonexistence; and the 10^2200 figure has no paper.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The acknowledgements and Conclusion of arXiv 2607.04365 (text beyond Section 11), to confirm or refute the ChatGPT 5.5 wording. (2) A compiled build of OPN-Proof1.lean and OPN-Proof2.lean (lake build against a pinned Mathlib), and the paper's own derivation of the reduced hypotheses from σ(N) = 2N. (3) A dated write-up of the 10^2200 computation from Ochem or Rao. (4) A named specialist's written assessment of the Reed, Shiraishi (18409975 and 18217948), Ortiz Hidalgo, Liu and Vega claims, or a published correction. (5) The Preprints.org record for Vega (dates, abstract and version history) and the Stone PDF. (6) The Elemente article's abstract and main theorem. (7) The author's response to the Pith objections for arXiv 2607.19746 and 2607.04365.

judgement.why: The statement asks only whether an odd perfect number exists. Unconditional nonexistence claims are scope whole but each is a self-published or unreviewed claim on a landmark problem, with no expert uptake, and later specialist work (Ochem–Zelinsky, Mantovanelli, July 2026) still treats the question as open. Several also carry their own signals: Shiraishi's scope ballooned and he conceded an earlier error, Reed's Lean files do not encode σ(N)=2N, and Liu's premise is incoherent. So all of these are not_credible. Results that settle nonexistence for a class of N are case: smallest prime factor in {5,…,17} (Mantovanelli), the form 13⁵m² (Shiraishi), and few distinct prime factors (Nielsen). Mantovanelli is credible-but-unreviewed: the only objections come from an AI referee. Necessary conditions that hold inside a class without excluding it are none (Yamada, Zelinsky, Stone, Ochem–Zelinsky). That means divisibility, reciprocal-sum bounds and smallest-prime bounds stated in terms of ω. So are conditional proofs (Vega 2022, Figshare, Rodgers) and unread or framework items (Mayo, Bërdëllima). Size lower bounds on N are finite checks, so instances. Tóth is about multiperfect/spoof numbers, so variant. Mantovanelli's acknowledgement (known only from a snippet) describes ChatGPT 5.5 doing formatting, search, presentation and coding support. Nothing places it in the mathematics, so ai_role is none. Vega 2024 has a year-only 2024 date, so after_snapshot is null.
judgement.doubts: Mantovanelli's AI disclosure is from an unverified snippet; 'coding support' for the verifier scripts that the closures rest on could, if substantive, merit 'assisted' — the record does not establish that. Treating Nielsen's ω lower bounds as 'case' versus 'none' is a judgement call (pre-snapshot, so it does not affect status). Bërdëllima may contain restricted-form nonexistence cases, but the record does not establish them.
judgement.by: judging pass (JUDGE.md), claude-opus-5-5; not the researching agent and not a human reviewer
